corpus_definition: Soft, thick hair taken from sheep to make clothes.

forms.definition: the soft, thick hair of sheep, used to make clothes and blankets
forms.example: This warm sweater is made of wool from Karakalpak sheep.

syn.note: Fleece is the whole coat of hair on a sheep before it is cut; also a soft modern fabric.
Yarn is long thread for knitting; it can be made of sheep hair, cotton or plastic.
Another natural material for clothes, but it comes from a plant, not an animal.

forms.note: There is no common verb made from this word.

forms.definition: made of the soft hair of sheep
forms.example: My grandmother knitted me woollen socks for the winter.
forms.note: British spelling: woollen; American spelling: woolen.

syn.note: Knitted clothes are made with long needles; they are often, but not always, made of sheep hair.

ant.note: Synthetic cloth is made from man-made materials, not from an animal.

forms.definition: covered with soft, thick hair, or made of it
forms.example: He wore a woolly hat when we went to Chimgan in January.
forms.note: American spelling: also wooly. In informal English it can also mean 'not clear' about ideas.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My aunt in Nukus buys wool at the bazaar every autumn. She makes woollen scarves for the whole family, and the children love their woolly hats.

reviewer_note: Spelling trap: British woollen/woolly vs American woolen/wooly; no affix claimed because -en is not in the affix table and the -y split doubles the l.

corpus_definition: To have a specific job or role.
usage_note: work as + a/an + job noun: 'She works as a nurse.' Don't forget the article: 'work as a teacher', not 'work as teacher'.

relations.note: Same meaning but more formal, used in letters and CVs.
Very easy: 'She is a nurse' means almost the same as 'She works as a nurse'.
Formal; used for an official role, often for a short time: 'He served as mayor.'

context.text: My cousin works as a doctor in a hospital in Tashkent. Before that, she worked as a teacher for two years.

reviewer_note: Article trap for Uzbek/Russian speakers: work as + a/an + job.

corpus_definition: To have a person or company as your boss.
particle_note: Not separable: 'work for a bank', 'work for my uncle'. Compare: work at + place ('work at a bank'), work for + company or person.

relations.note: Same meaning, more formal.
Work at names the place where you work; work for names who pays you.
The other side: a company employs you, and you work for the company.

context.text: Aziz works for a big phone company in Tashkent. His sister worked for the same company before she started her own business.

reviewer_note: Verb + preposition kept as phrasal per kind_hint; work for vs work at explained.

corpus_definition: To find the answer to a problem.
particle_note: Separable: 'work out the answer' or 'work the answer out'; with a pronoun always 'work it out'. Often + wh-clause: 'work out how to do it'.

relations.note: Same meaning, common in American English.
Used with problems and puzzles; a little more formal.
Only for numbers: find an answer using maths.
Easy word; work out means you reach understanding after thinking.

context.text: Dilnoza could not work out the last maths problem. Her brother helped her, and together they worked it out in five minutes.

reviewer_note: Map keeps only the 'find the answer' sense; the exercise sense (work out at the gym) is a different meaning and is not mixed in.

corpus_definition: The time of day you spend doing your job.
usage_note: Plural noun: 'My working hours are nine to five.' Common with during / outside / long / flexible: 'outside working hours'.

relations.note: Same meaning, more common in American English.
The hours when an office is open; used for office jobs.
A shift is one fixed period of work, often in a hospital or factory, sometimes at night.
The time when you are not working and can do what you like.

context.text: My working hours are from nine to six, Monday to Friday. My boss never calls me outside working hours.

reviewer_note: Fixed noun phrase; plural verb agreement noted.

corpus_definition: A small animal with a long, thin, soft body.

forms.definition: a small animal with a long, thin, soft body and no legs
forms.example: The bird pulled a worm out of the wet grass.

syn.note: A caterpillar looks a little similar but has legs and later becomes a butterfly.
A maggot is a very small young fly that looks like a tiny white worm.

forms.definition: to move slowly by twisting and pushing through a small space
forms.example: The boy wormed his way through the crowd to the front.
forms.note: Belongs to worm = moving slowly and carefully like this animal, not the animal itself. Usually 'worm your way'.
No common adjective; 'wormy' exists but is rare for learners.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: After the rain, many worms came out of the ground in our garden in Fergana. My little brother picked up a worm and gave it to the chickens.

reviewer_note: Compounds (earthworm, silkworm) left out per rule 7; same-spelling verb is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: To feel unhappy because you feel something bad might happen.
particle_note: Not separable: worry about + noun / -ing / wh-clause: 'worry about money', 'worry about failing', 'worry about what people think'. Also: be worried about.

relations.note: Same meaning; describes the state rather than the action.
A bit stronger and more formal; you feel nervous too.
Informal, common with young people: 'Don't stress about it.'
Care about means something is important to you; it doesn't mean you are afraid.
To feel calm and stop thinking about problems.

context.text: My mother always worries about me when I travel to Samarkand alone. I tell her not to worry about anything, because I call her every evening.

reviewer_note: Verb + preposition kept as phrasal per kind_hint; worry about vs care about contrasted.

corpus_definition: To put words on paper so that you do not forget them.
particle_note: Separable: 'write down the number' or 'write the number down'; with a pronoun always 'write it down'.

relations.note: Same meaning; often for short information.
Write something quickly and in a short form.
Write what someone is saying while they speak.
More formal; keep information on paper or a computer.

context.text: The teacher said, 'Write down your homework before you leave.' I wrote it down in my notebook so I would not forget.

reviewer_note: No true antonym, so the list has none.

usage_note: have / build / keep + a (good, close) relationship with + person: 'She has a close relationship with her grandmother.' For two sides together: a relationship between A and B.

relations.note: More general; can be between people, places or ideas.
Plural and more formal; often between groups or countries.
A strong feeling of love or friendship that joins people.
One kind of relationship, between friends.

context.text: Jasur has a very good relationship with his boss. He also wants to build a better relationship with his younger brother.

reviewer_note: Preposition trap: relationship with a person, relationship between two people.

corpus_definition: to leave a person or place forever without intending to return

forms.definition: the act of leaving a person or place forever
forms.example: The abandonment of the old factory left the town very quiet.

syn.note: Very close; often used for leaving a husband, wife, family or the army.

forms.definition: a feeling of being free, with no worry about rules
forms.example: The children danced with wild abandon at the wedding.
forms.note: Belongs to abandon = stop controlling yourself, not leaving a place. Usually in 'with (wild) abandon'.

forms.definition: to go away from a person or place and never come back
forms.example: The family had to abandon their house when the river flooded.

syn.note: Easy, general word; abandon means you leave forever and don't care what happens next.
Very close; often about leaving people who need you.
Easy phrase; you go and the person or thing stays.
Informal; used for leaving a partner or family suddenly.

ant.note: To remain in a place or with a person.

forms.definition: left empty or alone by the people who owned or cared for it
forms.example: We found an abandoned puppy near the bus stop.

syn.note: Very close; used most for places with no people.
Easy word; empty means no one is there now, maybe only for a short time.
Used for buildings that are empty and in bad condition.

ant.note: Used about a house or building where people are living or working.

forms.note: There is no common adverb in this family.

context.text: Many families abandoned their village in the mountains when the road closed. Today you can still see the abandoned houses. The abandonment of small villages worries local officials.

reviewer_note: Noun 'abandon' (with wild abandon) is a different meaning, shown as other_meaning extra; map keeps the 'leave forever' sense.
